why: A file that EXISTS and cannot be read can never become N/A, because N/A leaves the denominator and the score GOES UP. The old `lerJson` merged "does not exist" with "exists and is broken" into a `catch { return null }`, and `pkg === null` became `na('not an npm project')`. Measured in the attack: a repository at 9 of 10 (90%) with a syntactically broken package.json became 6 of 6 (100%) — dependabot, ci-gateia, typecheck and formatter vanished from the score and it started taking maximum marks. Breaking the file improved the score. The `fail` side HAS prettier, declared in apps/web/package.json, and even so it has to fail: what could not be read is not certified. It is that presence that makes the proof bite. Without it, the first version of this case stayed green under the mutation that gave the leniency back — the union of dependencies came out empty and the rule failed for the wrong reason, proving nothing. With it, both the old behavior (N/A, exit 0) and the half fix (skip the unreadable one and pass on the rest, exit 0) make this side diverge. The two trees are identical except for the trailing comma and the brace that does not close at the root.
